title: How steps grow
summary: Loops inside loops are O(n²), halving is O(log n), and Big-O keeps only the shape.

say.never: A loop *inside* another loop multiplies. Say you want to know whether any two students in a class of `n` share a birthday, so you compare every student with every other student. The outer loop runs `n` times, and *each time* the inner loop runs `n` times. That's `n × n` steps, written **O(n²)**, "n squared". Double the class and the work goes up four times.
say.bit: Nested loops over the same list multiply: **O(n²)**. Double `n`, four times the steps.

say.never: Some code throws away half of what's left at every step. Think of guessing a number from 1 to 1000 when someone says "higher" or "lower": each guess cuts the range in half, so about 10 guesses always find it. Double the range to 2000 and you need just *one* more guess. That's **O(log n)**, "log n". It barely grows at all.
say.bit: Halving what's left each step is **O(log n)**: double `n`, one more step.

say.never: Big-O ignores small details. Two loops one *after* the other are `n + n` steps: still a straight line, so still O(n). A loop that always runs 7 times is O(1), even when the list is huge, because it never runs more. And watch for **hidden loops**: `contains()` on an `ArrayList` checks the list item by item, so it is a loop even though you can't see one.
say.bit: Drop the constants: `2n` is O(n), a fixed 7 steps is O(1). `ArrayList.contains` is a hidden O(n) loop.

Double: `LINEAR`. Four times: `N_SQUARED`. Look out for a loop that doesn't depend on `n`, two loops in a row, and a `contains()` call.
